clinicalPearls: Age-related redundancy and laxity of eyelid skin, with weakening of the orbital septum and herniation of orbital fat
Very common in older adults and usually affects the upper lids most noticeably
Excess upper lid tissue can droop over the lashes and obscure the superior visual field
It is distinct from ptosis (a low lid margin) and from blepharochalasis (recurrent inflammatory episodes)
Superior visual field testing can document functional impairment to justify surgery
Blepharoplasty is the treatment when there is functional or significant cosmetic concern
reference.pathophysiology: Dermatochalasis results from age-related degeneration of eyelid skin and supporting tissues, with loss of skin elasticity, attenuation of the orbital septum and pseudoherniation of orbital fat. Gravity and chronic sun exposure contribute to the redundant, lax skin. The excess upper eyelid tissue can hang over the lid margin and lashes, mechanically limiting the superior visual field, while lower-lid changes are largely cosmetic.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment distinguishing skin redundancy from ptosis and brow ptosis
Superior visual field testing to document functional impairment
Assessment of levator function and lid crease
Exclusion of thyroid and other secondary causes of lid change
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or asymmetric changes suggesting another cause
Lesions suggesting eyelid neoplasm within redundant skin
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and slowly progressive; blepharoplasty reliably improves the visual field and appearance, though ageing changes may continue.
pitfalls: Mistaking coexisting ptosis or brow ptosis for simple dermatochalasis
Attributing all upper-lid heaviness to skin when the brow is the problem
Missing an eyelid tumour hidden within redundant folds
management: Offer upper-lid blepharoplasty with excision of redundant skin and pseudoherniated orbital fat for functional visual-field impairment or significant cosmetic concern
Document functional impairment with superior visual-field testing to justify surgical intervention
Identify and address coexisting brow ptosis with a brow lift, and distinguish and manage true ptosis where present
Exclude secondary causes such as thyroid eye disease before surgery
Observe mild or asymptomatic cases conservatively as the condition is benign
Refer to oculoplastic surgery and monitor postoperatively
